title: Notice how words and pictures build a story
intro: I can explain a word choice and a picture clue that help create a character, setting or event.
exampleTitle: Words tell an action; the picture adds a place
example: The words “Mae read” name the action. In the supplied illustration, the open book fits that action and shelves of books suggest a library setting. The plant adds a detail the sentence does not name. We can explain those visible choices without inventing the book’s title or Mae’s thoughts.
steps: 1. Link words with visible clues
Read the words and inspect the actual picture. Say what each contributes. Authors choose language; illustrators choose images, and sometimes one creator does both jobs.
Words: “Mae read.” Use the illustration directly below.
What does the picture add that these two words leave out?
The shelves of books suggest a library; the plant is another visible detail. Explain the contribution rather than only naming the illustrator’s job.
2. Explain a character or setting choice
Actions and speech can suggest a quality. Place and time words create a setting. Keep a supported interpretation separate from a fact.
Original story: “At dusk, Pip the duck gave a scarf to a shivering rabbit. ‘You can use mine,’ said Pip.” Dusk means the light is fading near the end of the day.
Which choice suggests that Pip is helpful? What human-like action has the writer given the duck?

Giving the scarf and offering its use suggest help. Speaking and lending clothing are human-like story actions, rather than evidence about how real ducks behave. At dusk gives a time clue; no place is named.
3. Compare real creators’ choices

Use actual picture books across First Nations Australian, other Australian and world creators. Compare a specific word or picture choice and explain its effect. One invented example does not replace this reading.

Adult supplies lawful illustrated copies of Little Bird’s Day (Sally Morgan and Johnny Warrkatja Malibirr), Time for Bed (Mem Fox and Jane Dyer), and Dear Zoo (Rod Campbell), or verified equivalent selections. Read and show the actual pages first.
Choose two actual pages. What does a word choice help you imagine, and what does the picture add?

Accept an explanation tied to visible details and real wording in each selected book. Identify title, author and illustrator. Different supported responses are welcome; do not infer cultural symbolism, reproduce artwork or treat one book as representing a whole culture.
mistakes: “The picture proves every thought.”
Describe the visible clue and say what it may suggest.
“A real animal always acts like its story character.”
Talking or wearing clothes may be an author’s imaginative choice.
“Knowing the creator’s name completes the discussion.”
Explain what the actual language and image choices do.
activity: Use two actual pages from the adult-supplied books named above. Name a character, place or event. Point to one language choice and one image detail on each page, then discuss a similarity or difference. Revisit the third creator context in another short session.
adjust: Starter: adult reads a page and offers two visible clues. Core: explain what a word and image each add. Stretch: compare how two creators build a similar moment, using evidence from both.
safety: The published books and their artwork are not included. Follow publisher and community guidance. Record the actual discussion and support; a correct written choice cannot establish this literature experience.
tricky: 1. Can one person be author and illustrator?
Yes. Explain the two jobs without assuming two different people must do them.
2. Does a moon prove an exact clock time?
No. It may suggest night in context, but an exact time needs more information.
3. Must all readers describe a character in the same way?
No. Different interpretations can be reasonable when the actual words and pictures support them.
faq: Can an adult read the book aloud?
Yes. The child can discuss the language and pictures without decoding every word independently.
Are the original mini-stories enough for this whole code?
They support the skill. Actual illustrated literature across the required creator contexts is also needed.
modelCaption: Words and illustration contribute different clues
modelCards: Explain the action and suggested setting

title: Connect a story with your own experience
intro: I can share a response to a literary text and explain a safe connection to my own experience.
example: Original story: “Nia waited for the swing. At last it was her turn. She grinned.” A reader might connect this with waiting for a game: both involve finally getting a turn. That memory can help explain a response to Nia; it does not tell us new facts about her.
steps: 1. Start with a real text detail
Name what happens before adding your memory. Ask a question about the character, setting or event and check what the words answer.
Original story: “Tom dropped his pencil. Ada lent him one. Tom smiled.”
Who helps Tom, and which words tell you? What could you ask about the event?
Ada helps: “Ada lent him one.” A question such as “Why might Tom smile?” invites a supported inference. His exact thoughts and the pencil’s colour are not stated.
2. Explain the shared experience
A useful connection links an event, feeling or idea with a safe experience you choose to share. Explain the shared part; the details need not match exactly.
Story: “Lena tried again when her tower fell.” Model connection: “I kept trying a puzzle when it was hard.”
What do the two experiences share? Make a safe connection of your own if you wish.

Both involve continuing after difficulty. Accept a relevant voluntary own-experience connection and explanation. An imagined example supports participation when needed, but does not demonstrate a personal memory.
3. Share and listen to different responses
A reader may enjoy a moment that worries another reader. Point back to the text and explain your response, then listen and ask a related question.
Original poem: “Rain taps the path. I splash and spin. My socks get wet. I hurry in.”
Which part interests you? Draw or act it, then explain a safe connection and ask your partner about their response.

Accept a response linked to a stated line and a relevant voluntary experience. A child may like splashing or dislike wet socks. Observe the actual exchange; a drawing alone does not show discussion. The voice saying I is the poem’s speaker, not necessarily its author.
mistakes: “My memory changes what happened.”
Keep the story’s details and your own experience separate.
“We must all feel the same.”
Explain different responses with relevant details.
“I must share something private.”
Choose an ordinary safe memory or decline; an adult can support a later comfortable connection.
activity: Read the complete rain poem above with a partner. Choose one line, explain your response and connect it with a safe experience. Listen to a different response and ask one related question. A drawing or role-play may support the explanation.
adjust: Starter: adult rereads one line and offers a connection stem. Core: link a text detail with a voluntary experience and explain. Stretch: compare two responses or discuss how the same memory connects differently with two actual texts.
safety: Never require private disclosure or agreement. An adult may read, sign or scribe. Record actual discussion and the assistance used; supported participation is not independent reading.
tricky: 1. Is owning a pencil always a useful connection to a helping story?
It is only a surface match unless you explain how it helps you understand the event or your response.
2. Can similar experiences have different details?
Yes. Waiting for a swing and waiting for a game can share the experience of waiting for a turn.
3. Does I in a poem prove the author experienced it?
No. The speaker can be imagined. Use what the text actually gives.
faq: Does there have to be one correct personal answer?
No. Accept different relevant connections with an explanation.
What if the child has no matching memory?
Use a safe known or imagined example for participation, and revisit an own-experience connection when appropriate. Record that boundary honestly.
modelCaption: Text detail → safe connection → explained response
modelCards: I remember waiting for a game.
Both involve waiting, then joining in.

title: Talk about who, where and what happens
intro: I can discuss characters, settings and connected events using clues from a story.
exampleTitle: A solution needs to address the problem
example: Original story: “After lunch, Tia took seedlings into the yard. Her watering can leaked. Dad brought a jug, and Tia watered the seedlings.” Tia and Dad are characters; the yard after lunch is the setting. The leak creates a problem, and the jug helps solve it by holding water.
steps: 1. Separate the story features
Ask who is involved, where and when it happens, and what happens. A character can be an animal or imagined being that takes part. Do not turn every named object into a character.
Original story: “On Saturday morning, Bo returned a book to the library. The librarian thanked Bo.”
Name a character, the place, the time and an event.
Bo and the librarian are characters. The place is the library and the time is Saturday morning. Returning the book or thanking Bo is an event. The book is an object in this story.
2. Connect the problem, action and result
A problem gets in the way of a goal. Explain why an action helps. Some stories give a sequence without a stated problem; do not invent one.
A: “Ari could not reach the ball under a bench. Jo rolled it out with a stick. Ari picked it up.” B: “Mia picked a flower, placed it in a jar and put the jar on a table.”
What solves A’s problem? Is a problem stated in B?
Rolling the ball out makes it reachable. B tells connected events without a stated problem. Keep each retelling in its own order rather than forcing both into one pattern.
3. Compare places and character choices
Use actual clues when comparing stories, narrative poems or fables. A familiar place can contain imagined events. A character’s action may affect what happens next.
A: “In a city garden, a mouse thanked a talking tree for shelter.” B: “On a country path, a child thanked a neighbour for an umbrella.”
What is similar? What differs? Which detail is imagined?

Both show thanks for help with shelter. The characters, places and helping objects differ. A talking tree is an imagined feature; the garden is a familiar kind of place. No season or exact year is given. Later compare an actual adult-supplied traditional tale or fable with another familiar story.
mistakes: “A setting is something that happens.”
A setting tells where or when; an event tells what happens.
“Every ending solves every problem.”
Check whether the action addresses the obstacle.
“Every story must state a problem.”
Discuss the connected events the actual text gives.
activityTitle: Make a story map and discuss it
activity: Adult reads this original story: “Before breakfast, Lee took a kite into the yard. Its ribbon caught on a chair. Lee loosened the ribbon and flew the kite.” Use three headings: Who? Where/when? What happens? Retell the events and explain how Lee’s action helps.
adjust: Starter: adult rereads and offers two feature choices. Core: name features and show their clues. Stretch: explain a cause or compare features in two actual familiar literary texts.
safety: Accept spoken, signed, AAC, drawn or scribed explanations. Use actual complete texts for comparisons. Assess discussion of features separately from handwriting and independent decoding.
tricky: 1. Does Saturday morning tell where?
No. It tells when. A place clue answers where.
2. Can a realistic setting appear in a fantasy?
Yes. A talking tree can appear in a city garden; discuss each actual clue.
3. Is an object always a character?
No. Check its role. An imagined speaking book could be a character, while a book being returned can simply be an object.
faq: Must a child use formal plot terms?
No. Who, where, when and what happens are useful Year 1 language.
Can there be more than one useful retelling?
Yes. Accept faithful main events and relevant extra details when their order and connections remain clear.
modelCaption: Who? Where and when? What happens?

title: Hear, echo and invent sound patterns
intro: I can listen to a literary sound pattern, imitate it and invent a meaningful new version.
example: Adult reads the original lines aloud: “Small snails slide. We see a bee beside a tree.” Small/snails/slide repeat the beginning /s/ sound. Bee/tree have matching spoken endings. Say the whole lines for meaning before comparing their different sound patterns.
steps: 1. Hear the part that matches
Alliteration repeats a beginning sound in nearby words. Rhyme matches spoken endings in different words. Listen; spelling alone cannot decide either pattern.
Adult says: “Big bears bounce.” Then says cat, hat and cup.
Which beginning sound repeats in the line? Which two words rhyme?
Big/bears/bounce begin with /b/. Cat/hat rhyme; cat/cup share a beginning but have different endings. Adult models the actual sounds and accepts pronunciation differences with appropriate guidance.
2. Echo and choose an effect
Listen first, then echo a poem, chant or song. Pace, volume and pauses can change an effect. Keep any movement comfortable and optional.

Original chant: “Tap, tap, rest. Tap, tap, rest.” Adult says it gently, then with a livelier steady pulse. For a song, adult sings “We can play, come this way” to do–re–mi, mi–re–do, one word per beat at a comfortable pitch.
Echo one model. Which delivery do you choose, and how does it fit?

Accept a deliberate gentle or lively choice with an explanation or indication. Observe actual listening and echoing. The song has play/way rhyme; the chant repeats its words. Written recognition does not demonstrate singing or imitation.
3. Invent and discuss a new line
Change a heard pattern while keeping a sensible meaning. A new line can use a different word pair or action. Tell a listener what you kept and changed.
Original model: “A goat floats in a boat.” Goat/boat rhyme. Another model is “Little lizards leap,” with a returning /l/ beginning.
Invent a different rhyming or alliterative line, say or communicate it, and explain its pattern.

For example, “A cat sits on a mat” rhymes, or “Little lambs listen” repeats /l/. Accept another meaningful creation. A copied model is imitation; a genuine new choice shows invention. Do not require one exact line or a technical definition.
mistakes: “Same letter always means same sound.”
Listen to the actual beginning; an adult can model spelling contrasts.
“The same word repeated supplies a new rhyming word.”
Name repetition separately from a different word with a matching ending.
“Louder is always better.”
Choose a voice that fits the text and listener.
activityTitle: Hear it, change it, share it
activity: Adult reads this original model: “Sleepy seals slide by the sea.” Echo it, then create a different meaningful line with a repeated beginning sound. Share it with a partner and discuss what repeats. Use the actual adult-sung six-word model in focus 2 for an optional new song version.
adjust: Starter: echo a short adult model and choose between two heard words. Core: imitate, make a meaningful change and share it. Stretch: compare delivery effects or combine rhyme with repetition, within familiar language.
safety: Actual listening and response are needed. Use authorised First Nations Australian performances, Asian poetry/chants/songs and familiar-topic haiku in wider reading with their creator, language and context identified. Original neutral verse does not replace these cultural selections. The retained guide gives preparation guidance.
tricky: 1. Are cat and cup a rhyming pair?
No. They begin alike, but their spoken endings differ.
2. Must syllables always get one beat each?
No. A steady beat and the word syllables can differ. The short teaching tune assigns one word per beat only for that model.
3. Does saying a copied line prove invention?
It shows imitation. A meaningful new word or line is needed to show an original change.
faq: Does the child need formal music notation?
No. The tune guide supports the adult, who models the actual song first.
Do we require a perfect performance?
No. Notice the intended sound pattern, meaningful change, discussion and access support; do not demand perfect pitch or a particular accent.
modelCaption: Beginning sounds and ending sounds are different patterns

title: Retell a story and make a new version
intro: I can retell important events and deliberately adapt a familiar story while keeping it clear.
exampleTitle: Keep the links that explain the ending
example: Read this original story together until familiar: “Sam took a ball to the park. It rolled under a bench. Jo used a stick to roll it out. Sam thanked Jo, and they played.” A short retelling keeps the stuck ball and Jo’s help because they explain how play resumes. The exact wording can change.
steps: 1. Keep the important sequence
Hear the whole story more than once, then choose events a listener needs. A retelling keeps its main meaning; it is more than a list of objects.
Original story: “Nell planted a seed. She watered the soil. A shoot appeared.” Read or hear it twice before retelling.
Tell the important events in order. Can the shoot appear first in an accurate retelling of this version?
Nell plants the seed, waters the soil, and a shoot appears. An accurate retelling keeps this supplied order. The learner tells it; recognising a correct order on paper is only support.
2. Make characters and language clear
Name who acts, keep pronouns clear and use story words or a little dialogue. A listener can follow the meaning without a memorised script.
Original story: “Sam could not reach his ball. Jo rolled it out with a stick. ‘Thank you, Jo,’ said Sam.”
Describe Jo using an action clue. Say Sam’s thanks in a way that fits the event.

Jo is helpful because Jo retrieves the ball. Accept a clear character description and a spoken, signed or accessible expression of thanks. Observe the actual retelling or role-play; spelling and accent are separate from the story meaning.
3. Adapt deliberately and check the links
Say what you will change. Keep enough plot, characters, language or structure for the familiar story to be recognisable, and adjust linked details so the new version makes sense.
Familiar version: a ball rolls under a park bench and Jo uses a stick to retrieve it. Planned adaptation: move the event to a classroom.
Tell an adapted version. Which objects or actions might need changing?

For example, the ball rolls under a desk and Jo uses a ruler to roll it out, then Sam gives thanks. Accept another coherent version. One change is a manageable starting point, not a rule limiting every adaptation.
mistakes: “Retelling means repeating every word.”
Use your own clear words while preserving the important events.
“Any forgotten event is an adaptation.”
Ask what changed on purpose and whether the new links work.
“A plan or selected answer proves oral retelling.”
Listen to the learner tell or communicate the actual story.
activityTitle: Three pictures, then a fresh telling
activity: Read the complete Sam and Jo story in the worked example together twice. The child draws three simple planning pictures, retells it to a listener, then announces one change and tells an adapted version. Compare what stayed and what changed.
adjust: Starter: adult models, then offers three event prompts. Core: retell connected events and a clear finish. Stretch: adapt a character or setting and explain the linked changes; add fitting dialogue or a short character description.
safety: Drawing, role-play, signing, AAC, a scribe or an optional recording can support communication. Observe the actual targeted performance and note help. Use actual familiar texts; no special device or private experience is required.
tricky: 1. Can you leave out the colour of the ball?
Usually, if that detail does not explain the important events in the chosen version.
2. Can you leave out the helper when the helper retrieves it?
That may break the explanation of the ending. Keep the event that connects the problem and result.
3. Must every object stay unchanged in an adaptation?
No. Deliberate changes can work when the version stays recognisable and the linked events make sense.
faq: Must it be written?
No. Oral telling is central; drawing, writing or digital tools can support it.
How familiar should the story be?
Read or hear it several times and discuss its meaning before expecting a retelling from memory or a plan.
modelCaption: Retell the connected story; announce a deliberate change

title: Find a text’s job from its clues
intro: I can discuss what a text is for and explain how its words and features help.
exampleTitle: The same topic can serve different jobs
example: A: “Jo flew a kite. A gust lifted it above the tree.” B: “Kites have a frame and a covering.” Both concern kites. A tells events about Jo; B gives information. The topic alone cannot tell us the purpose.
steps: 1. Read the whole message
Ask what the reader is meant to know, do or enjoy. A text can tell events, share facts, give steps, invite or encourage a choice. Use complete messages as evidence.
A: “Come to our class show on Friday at 2 pm in the hall.” B: “Our class performed a show in the hall yesterday.”
Which invites the reader, and which tells about an event?
A invites: Come plus event, time and place help people attend. B reports an event. Both mention a show and hall; those shared topic words do not settle the job.
2. Explain how a feature helps
A heading names a topic, a list can name materials, and ordered actions can guide a task. Similar purposes often use similar patterns, but check the words.
Make a name card. You need paper and a pencil. 1. Fold the paper. 2. Write your name. 3. Stand the card on the table.
What does the materials list do? How do the numbered steps help?
The list names what is needed. The steps give actions in order. Their function matters; numbers alone could also organise events in a story.
3. Choose a text and justify it
Choose the message that helps with a real need. Name its job and a useful clue. Some messages combine information with an invitation or persuasion.
A: “Library closed today. Open again on Monday.” B: “Please visit our book stall on Saturday. Sales help buy class books.”
Which helps you decide when the library reopens? What two jobs can B do?
A gives Monday reopening information. B invites people to the stall and encourages support with a reason. Accept a main-purpose explanation or supported account of both jobs.
mistakes: “The topic tells the purpose.”
Compare what the full messages do with that topic.
“A poster always persuades.”
A poster can inform, warn, invite or persuade. Read its actual message.
“One feature is certain proof.”
Treat it as a clue and check the rest of the text.
activityTitle: Make two messages with different jobs
activity: With an adult, make two complete cards about a class garden. One shares a fact, such as “Plants need water.” The other asks for a helpful action with a reason. Read each to a partner and discuss how their words help different purposes.
adjust: Starter: adult reads two supplied messages and offers purpose words. Core: name the job and explain a feature. Stretch: compare a shared feature across different jobs or explain a message with two supported purposes.
safety: Adult read-aloud supports access; do not call that independent decoding. Use actual cards or complete supplied texts. This lesson concerns discussing purpose, not writing a long formal analysis.
tricky: 1. Does numbered text always give instructions?
No. Numbered sentences can tell events. Check whether they direct the reader to act.
2. Can facts support persuasion?
Yes. A relevant fact can give a reason for a requested choice.
3. Does a picture replace missing invitation details?
No. Check what, when and where in the actual message.
faq: Can a story be based on real events?
Yes. Its purpose can still be to tell a connected story.
Do we force one purpose label every time?
No. Explain the main job and recognise supported mixed purposes where relevant.

title: Listen, take turns and build a conversation
intro: I can share an understandable message, listen for meaning and add a connected idea or question.
exampleTitle: A pause can be thinking time
example: Mia says, “My tower fell because…” and pauses. Jo waits. Mia adds, “…the base was too small.” Jo asks, “Could we make a wider base?” Jo listens to the complete idea and builds on it instead of filling the pause with an unrelated topic.
steps: 1. Share a fair turn
Agree on a useful signal and leave thinking time. If two people start together, pause and repair the overlap. A relevant response shows more than waiting silently.
Partner A: “I want a quiet game.” Partner B: “We could try a puzzle. Would that suit you?”
Practise a short exchange about a game. How will you repair speaking together?

Observe an actual exchange with a connected reply. “Please finish; I will wait” is one useful repair. Accept access supports and a choice to pass; do not supply the child’s contribution then call it independent.
2. Make meaning clear and check it
Use precise words, a suitable pace and a comfortable volume. Repeat, reword or use a communication support if needed. A listener can restate or ask for clarification.
Materials: paper and pencil. Adult says, “Draw a small circle beside a large square.” Listener checks, “Small circle beside large square—is that right?”
Give and follow a different simple drawing direction with a partner. Check what was understood.

Look for the stated size and position in the response and drawing. Clarification can be good listening. Observe actual speech where required; signing or AAC can communicate meaning while a speech-specific criterion remains unobserved.
3. Add a useful question or response

Stay connected to the last contribution. Ask for the detail you need, offer a reason or build a plan that considers different ideas. Open questions can invite explanation; closed questions can check a detail.
Visitor role-play: “I grow vegetables.” Ask “What do you grow?” Adult replies, “Beans.”
Ask a follow-up based on that reply. Then try a yes/no question that checks a detail.

For example, “How do you look after the beans?” and “Do you water them each day?” are connected. Listen to the actual answer before the next turn. Accept other relevant questions; do not judge a question only by its first word.
mistakes: “Eye contact proves listening.”
Check understanding through a relevant reply, restatement or question.
“Everyone must speak on command.”
Allow thinking time, different communication modes and a choice to pass.
“Louder fixes every unclear message.”
Check wording, pace, noise and the listener’s needs; avoid shouting.
activity: With a partner, choose a place to read. One wants quiet and the other wants room to sit together. Take turns, respond to both needs, ask a useful question and check the agreed plan. At home, the partner can be an adult.
adjust: Starter: offer a topic and one talk stem. Core: exchange turns, make a clear message and give a related reply. Stretch: combine two suggestions or respectfully disagree with a reason and a follow-up.
safety: Observe the real exchange and note context, communication mode and prompts. Accent, dialect, eye contact and stillness are not behaviour scores. Written choices alone cannot establish conversation performance.
tricky: 1. Must you agree to respond well?
No. A different view can be helpful when it is connected, respectful and explained.
2. Is every pause an invitation to interrupt?
No. The speaker may be thinking. Wait or check whether the turn is finished.
3. Can a short yes/no question be useful?
Yes. It can check a missing detail; open questions can invite a fuller explanation.
faq: Can signing or AAC support participation?
Yes. Record how meaning was communicated and any speech-specific skill that was not observed.
How do we tell whether someone listened?
Look for a response that uses the partner’s meaning, including a relevant clarification question.
modelCaption: Wait for meaning; add a connected contribution
modelCards: Mia: The base was too small.
Jo: Could we make it wider?

title: Compare story, information and persuasive texts
intro: I can explain a similarity and a difference between texts and choose one for a purpose.
exampleTitle: Three messages about the same subject
example: A: “The moon put a cloud in its pocket.” B: “The moon can be seen in the night sky.” C: “Look at the moon tonight; you may notice its shape.” A invents a human-like action, B gives information, and C encourages an action while also sharing information. Explain clues rather than sorting only by topic.
steps: 1. Read for the main job
An imaginative text can tell an invented story, which may be realistic or fantastic. An informative text helps us learn. A persuasive text tries to influence a choice, belief or action.
A writer invents: “Jo lost a hat at the oval and found it by the gate.” An information card says: “A hat can shade your face.”
Must A be information because the events could happen? What useful information does B give?
No. A is explicitly an invented story with connected events. B explains a use of a hat. Possible events and real objects can appear in invented stories.
2. Compare what both include and what differs
Say something supported by both messages, then compare what they do. A fact can also support a request, so purposes can overlap.
A: “Plants need water.” B: “Please water our plants so they do not dry out.”
What do both concern? What does B ask the reader to do that A does not?
Both concern plants and water. B asks for watering and gives a reason. A shares information without that request. The shared topic does not make the whole messages identical.
3. Choose for a stated task
Use the complete text and actual image clues. Headings, photographs and story pictures can occur in different text types; no single feature always proves purpose.
A: “Wombats dig burrows in the ground.” B: “Wally the wombat packed an umbrella and sailed away.” C: “Please protect wombat homes so wombats have shelter.”
Which helps find out where wombats live? Which gives an invented event? Which asks for an action?

A gives burrow information, B follows a character’s imagined adventure, and C asks for protection with a reason. For the first task, choose A and point to “burrows in the ground”. Discuss the actual messages rather than deciding from the animal alone.
mistakes: “Everything possible is an information text.”
Realistic events can be invented by a storyteller.
“Only stories can have pictures.”
Compare the actual words and image purpose; all these text types can use images.
“A text can do only one job.”
Explain its main job and any additional supported purpose.
activity: Adult writes three cards: “A fox packed a picnic and waved goodbye.” “Foxes have fur.” “Please close the picnic bin so animals cannot reach scraps.” Read them together. Discuss one shared topic connection, a difference in what each does and the best card for learning an animal fact.
adjust: Starter: adult reads two cards and offers purpose words. Core: give a supported similarity and difference. Stretch: explain how an information detail can support persuasion or why a plausible event can still be invented.
safety: Use complete actual texts and supplied pictures. Adult reading supports text comparison but is not independent reading evidence. Avoid long formal genre analysis or judging a family’s choices.
tricky: 1. Does an animal in a text make it factual?
No. Check whether it shares information, follows invented events or encourages a choice.
2. Is a shared title enough to prove the same purpose?
No. Read the messages and compare what they do.
3. Can two different text types share a fact?
Yes. A persuasive request may use a fact as its reason. Explain both the shared content and the difference in purpose.
faq: Must imaginative writing include magic?
No. A writer can invent everyday events.
What counts as a useful comparison?
Name a specific shared feature or idea and a difference supported by both actual texts.
modelCaption: One subject can support several text purposes
modelCards: Moon story: a cloud in its pocket

title: Read the words, check and reread
intro: I can use taught letter–sound knowledge, check the printed meaning and reread with clear phrasing.
example: Printed sentence: “The frog hops.” If a reader says “The flag hops”, return to the letters in frog: /f/ /r/ /o/ /g/. Blend the sounds, then reread the printed sentence and check its meaning. A picture can explain what a frog is; it cannot replace reading the word’s spelling.
steps: 1. Blend taught patterns in order
Use the letter–sound patterns already taught to the child. A digraph can use two letters for one sound. Blend through the whole word, then connect it with the sentence meaning.
Adult model: shop → /sh/ /o/ /p/. Fresh printed text: “The fish swims.” Adult teaches any unfamiliar word or spelling first.
Read fish. Which letters work together? Then read the whole short sentence.

The letters sh represent one sound in fish: /f/ /i/ /sh/. Listen to actual word and sentence reading. Supply help for untaught patterns, then try a suitable fresh example rather than judging unsupported decoding.
2. Read meaningful phrases and monitor
First read accurately, then group words that belong together. Punctuation helps show boundaries and expression. Use grammar and meaning to notice a mismatch, then return to the actual spelling.
Adult model: “The little dog / ran home.” The slash marks a practice phrase group, not punctuation. Fresh printed text: “Can the dog jump?”
Read the fresh question aloud. If you say bump instead of jump, how will you check it?

Read the question with natural phrasing. Return to jump and check j and the remaining letters, then reread. A plausible word is not enough: read the word that is printed. Do not insist on one exaggerated voice.
3. Correct, seek help and reread

When reading breaks down, check the letters and blend again. If needed, ask for help. Reread for accurate words, a suitable pace and meaning rather than racing. Authentic texts may contain untaught words needing adult support.
Original classroom notice with a real purpose: “Please close the gate. The dog is in the yard.” Adult supplies untaught words such as please before supported reading.
Read the notice with the support you need. What does it ask you to do? Then reread without changing the printed words.

It asks the reader to close the gate. Observe the actual supported reading, corrections, phrasing and meaning. Note supplied words and other help. Adult read-aloud comprehension or one word choice cannot establish independent fluency.
mistakes: “A picture tells me which word to guess.”
Look through the letters and blend; use the picture to support meaning.
“Fastest reading is best.”
Keep accurate words, meaningful phrases, a suitable pace and understanding.
“A supported notice is independently decoded.”
Record help and assess taught-pattern reading separately.
activity: Use the printed original text “The fish swims. The dog can jump.” Confirm or teach the needed correspondences and words first. Listen to a first reading, help with a specific difficulty, then invite a reread and a brief explanation of what each animal does.
adjust: Starter: adult models a word, blends with the child and supports a short phrase. Core: read suitable taught-pattern text, correct a mismatch and reread for meaning. Stretch: read a slightly longer familiar text or supported authentic notice with clear phrasing.
safety: Match texts to the child’s taught phonics and explain new vocabulary. Familiar high-frequency words still need their known spelling parts and any unusual parts taught. Observe reading itself, using appropriate access support and recording what was supplied.
tricky: 1. Can a correct picture choice prove reading?
No. It may show recognition or meaning. Hear or otherwise observe the child reading the actual printed text.
2. What if a guessed word makes sense?
Check all the letters anyway. More than one word can be plausible, but the spelling identifies the printed word.
3. Is asking for help a failure?
No. It is a useful strategy when checking and rereading do not resolve a difficulty. Record the support and practise the needed pattern.
faq: Is every Year 1 text independently decodable for every child?
No. Match the text with what that child has been taught; support untaught patterns and words.
Do grammar and context replace phonics?
No. Use them to monitor and check meaning while reading and correcting the actual printed words.
modelCaption: Printed word → ordered sounds → blend → check → reread

title: Use clues to build and check meaning
intro: I can use comprehension strategies and explain which clues support my understanding.
exampleTitle: A prediction can change when we read more
example: Original opening: “Dark clouds filled the sky. Jo took a raincoat.” Rain is a reasonable prediction because of the clouds and raincoat, but it is not certain. Next part: “The clouds passed. Jo carried the coat home in sunshine.” Read the new information and revise the prediction instead of ignoring it.
steps: 1. Picture, predict and check
Visualise what the words actually name. Before reading further, predict from a title, picture or text clue. Separate that prediction from what is already stated, then read on.
Original opening: “Two kittens sat under a bench. A dog came along the path.” Make a prediction before opening the answer to read the next part.
Name the details your mental picture must keep. Before hearing the next part, predict with a clue; then check it.

Keep two kittens, sitting under a bench, and a dog coming along a path. Different predictions are possible if explained. Next part: “The dog walked past, and the kittens stayed where they were.” Check your first idea against that new information. The words do not specify colours.
2. Connect and infer without claiming certainty
Link a text to relevant knowledge or experience. An inference uses a clue plus what you know; it is not a made-up fact. Read surrounding words to check new vocabulary.
A: “The path was slick after rain. It was easy to slip.” B: “Mia smiled when her friend arrived.”
What does slick mean here? What might Mia feel, and what is the clue?

Slick means slippery here: rain and “easy to slip” support it. Mia may feel pleased to see the friend; the smile is a clue, not certainty about every feeling. A relevant safe connection can help explain the idea without changing the text.
3. Summarise, question and find evidence

A summary keeps important ideas rather than every small detail. Ask questions and check whether the answer is stated, can be inferred or is not given. Build topic vocabulary before and during reading.
A seedling is a young plant. Original text: “Luca planted a seedling. The soil felt dry, so Luca watered it. Later the leaves looked firmer.”
Give a short summary. Ask a question the words answer. Do they tell the plant’s exact age?

For example, Luca waters a young plant when the soil is dry, and its leaves later look firmer. “Why did Luca water it?” is answered by the dry soil. Exact age is not given. Accept a faithful summary and another answerable question.
mistakes: “Every mental picture must look identical.”
Keep the named details; leave unstated colours or designs open.
“A prediction is already a fact.”
Explain the clue and check it against later information.
“The text answers every question.”
Say when information is missing instead of guessing it.
activity: Adult reads this original information text without pointing out the answers: “Beetles have six legs. Their hard wing covers protect their wings.” The learner recalls two details, explains what the text is mainly about and asks one answerable question. Reread for access if needed.
adjust: Starter: adult reads a short complete text and helps locate a clue. Core: use a strategy and explain evidence. Stretch: revise a prediction, distinguish stated/inferred/missing information or give a concise summary with a relevant question.
safety: Personal disclosure is optional. Record whether the learner listened, viewed or read and what help was given. A text can support several reasonable inferences; keep claims proportionate to its evidence. Do not score artistic skill or assume adult-read responses prove independent reading.
tricky: 1. Can a sensible prediction turn out wrong?
Yes. New information can change it; explain the clue and the revision.
2. Is one small detail always a summary?
No. A summary needs to keep what the whole short text is mainly about or its important connected events.
3. Must an inference be certain?
No. Use may or probably where appropriate and give the clue. Some questions cannot be answered from the supplied text.
faq: Can these strategies be used while listening or viewing?
Yes. Use actual spoken text or visible evidence and record that response route.
Does a connection have to reveal a private memory?
No. A safe relevant experience or known example can support understanding without private disclosure.
modelCaption: Clue → possible idea → new information → checked understanding
modelCards: Later: clouds pass; revise the idea
